title: Translation; Genes, the genetic code and genomes
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE03#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE03#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE03#t1 term and clue written for the game; GE05a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: GE03#N.3a, GE05a#N.4, GE03#N.5a, GE05a#N.7, GE05a#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Start codon
items.clue: AUG: sets where reading begins, and also specifies methionine.

items.label: Stop codon
items.clue: UAA, UAG or UGA: specifies no amino acid, so the polypeptide ends there.

items.label: Degenerate code
items.clue: Feature meaning that most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet.

items.label: Translation
items.clue: Using the base sequence of mRNA to build the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.

questions.explanation: 4 × 4 = 16 is fewer than 20; 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.

questions.explanation: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids; for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?

options.text: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the first nucleotide of the start codon to the last nucleotide of the stop codon, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does the polypeptide translated from this region contain?
questions.explanation: 903 ÷ 3 = 301 codons. AUG codes for methionine and the stop codon codes for nothing, so the polypeptide has 301 − 1 = 300 amino acids.
